Chapter 9: Competing in Fragmented, Emerging, and Global Industries
You know, not every industry plays by the same rules. Some markets are crowded with lots of small businesses, none really dominating. Others are just getting started, full of uncertainty and change. And then, there are those that stretch across the globe, weaving through different countries and cultures. Each of these situations calls for a different strategy, and that's what we're diving into right now.
Let’s start with fragmented industries. Think about places where no one company really stands out—like local restaurants, small retail shops, or many service providers. Competition is fierce, and making a big profit can be tough.
So, how do you succeed in a space like this? Well, one way is through consolidation—teaming up with, or even buying out, other businesses to get bigger and more efficient. Another option is to specialize. Maybe you focus on a unique market niche or offer something nobody else does. Or, you could go for standardization—creating a repeatable model, like franchising, so you can scale up quickly.
Picture a coffee shop chain that grows by acquiring independent cafés and streamlining everything so every location runs smoothly. That’s consolidation and standardization in action.
Now, what about emerging industries? These are the wild frontiers—places driven by innovation, uncertainty, and rapid growth. The rules aren’t set yet, and being early can give you a huge edge.
Here, you might want to shape the standards—think about setting the technology or safety benchmarks everyone else will have to follow. Or, focus on building your capabilities, like investing in research, finding great talent, or ramping up your infrastructure so you can grow fast. And don’t forget about managing all that uncertainty—flexible business models and a willingness to experiment can help you find what really works.
Take the electric vehicle market, for example. Companies are racing not just to sell cars, but to set the standards and become the go-to brand. It’s all about moving quickly and making smart bets.
Then, there are global industries. These operate across borders, facing all kinds of competitors, rules, and customer preferences.
Here’s where you need to think about adapting to each local market—maybe changing your products or how you market them to fit different cultures and regulations. At the same time, you can use your global size to lower costs and spread out your risks. But, of course, running a business across multiple countries adds a whole new layer of complexity. You’ve got to coordinate teams across time zones and manage all the moving parts.
Imagine a fast-food chain that tweaks its menu from country to country, making sure it fits local tastes, but still keeps that unmistakable brand feel. That’s global strategy in action.
So, what’s the key takeaway here? Every type of industry—fragmented, emerging, or global—brings its own set of challenges. If you want to succeed, you’ll need to really understand the landscape you’re in, and be ready to adapt your strategy as things change.
